newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain seeks stiff prison terms for pro-ETA violence.
newsitem.headline: Spain seeks stiff prison terms for pro-ETA violence.

text.p: The Spanish government has proposed stiff prison terms for Basque separatist supporters involved in street violence or illegal demonstrations, the daily El Pais newspaper reported on Friday.

The government drew up the proposed legal reforms as part of a pledged crackdown on the separatist guerrilla group ETA for killing Basque town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco last month. The assassination spurred massive demonstrations across Spain.

According to a leaked draft proposal published by EL Pais, the government is seeking 10- to 20-year prison terms for anyone who burns or destroys property and one to two years in jail for taking part in illegal demonstrations.

Radical youth groups who support ETA (Basque Homeland ands Freedom) regularly rampage through the streets of Basque towns, burning buses, phone boxes, automatic banking machines and other symbols of the Spanish state's authority.
Until now, street violence has only been penalised by jail terms if it endangered people, El Pais said.
The Interior Ministry has been circulating the draft among political parties in an effort to build a consensus in favour of the reforms.
An ministry spokesman would not comment on the authenticity of the published document but said it had been leaked to the press by a political party.

The document refers to frequent street violence in the Basque region by pro-ETA youths as "low intensity terrorism" used by the guerrilla group "to create a climate of violence and insecurity in the streets".

It also proposes prison sentences of up to two years for thnose who attend demonstrations with their faces masked. Those participating in counterdemonstrations could face up to 24 weekends in prison or a fine.
The reforms also seek speedy trials for street violence.
The government cautions in the document that legal reforms must be carried out "with extraordinary prudence".
Political analysts have said too tough a crackdown could increase public sympathy for ETA's claims that the government is authoritarian and represses basic liberties.
